title: Vitamin C and Cancer: The Route Changes Everything
hook: Linus Pauling was mocked for saying vitamin C fights cancer — because the trials used pills. Given intravenously it reaches concentrations that behave like a drug, not a vitamin.
key_points: Pauling's claim was dismissed after trials using vitamin C pills showed no benefit.
Oral absorption is capped, so pills can't reach high blood concentrations.
Intravenous delivery bypasses that limit and reaches vastly higher levels.
At those concentrations vitamin C acts more like an experimental drug than a supplement.
Early studies suggest it may damage vulnerable cancer cells and reduce treatment side effects.
It is still experimental — not an established cancer therapy.
content_html: Linus Pauling — two Nobel prizes, and by the end of his life a byword for scientific overreach — insisted vitamin C could fight cancer. Trials of vitamin C pills found nothing, and the claim became a cautionary tale.
extra_html:
As ScienceDaily reports, the modern understanding is that the trials tested the wrong thing. The gut caps how much vitamin C it will absorb, so no oral dose gets blood concentrations very high. Delivered intravenously, it bypasses that ceiling entirely and reaches levels an order of magnitude beyond anything a pill can achieve — and at those concentrations vitamin C stops behaving like a nutrient and starts behaving like a cytotoxic agent, generating oxidative stress that some cancer cells are unusually poor at handling.

Early studies suggest it may damage vulnerable tumour cells, reduce side effects of standard treatment, and possibly improve outcomes for some patients. "Suggest" and "some" are load-bearing: this is active research, not established care, and IV vitamin C is also heavily marketed by clinics well ahead of the evidence. The durable lesson is the pharmacological one — route and dose can change what a molecule does, and a failed trial sometimes tested a version of the idea that was never going to work.

related.title: A Surprising Link Between Vitamin C and Brain Health
related.hook: In a study of over 2,000 older adults, people with lower blood vitamin C had less gray matter and weaker brain connections tied to memory and attention.

related.title: A $70 Billion Industry With Thin Evidence
related.hook: Supplements are one of the fastest-growing corners of health spending. For most of what's on the shelf, there's little evidence it does what the label implies.

flashcards.prompt: Why did vitamin C pills fail in cancer trials while IV vitamin C looks different?
flashcards.back_html: Oral absorption is limited, so pills can't push blood levels very high. Intravenous delivery bypasses that ceiling and reaches vastly higher concentrations — where vitamin C behaves like an experimental drug.

flashcards.prompt: What's the general lesson from the vitamin C story?

choices.text: Route and dose can change what a substance does in the body
Any supplement will work if you take enough of it
Pauling was right and IV vitamin C is now standard cancer care

flashcards.explanation_html: The same molecule produced no benefit as a pill and shows drug-like activity by IV, because absorption capped the achievable concentration. That said, IV vitamin C remains experimental, not established therapy.
